<skill name="company-secure-delivery">
# Secure delivery

The dojo works on payment software with no real payments and no real data. These rules are
non-negotiable and hold in every stage, including tests, fixtures, documentation and manifests.

## Data

- Synthetic data only, and obviously fake: test IBANs from the reserved ranges, names like
  `Test Debtor 01`, amounts that no one could mistake for a real transaction.
- Never copy a value from a production system, a ticket, a screenshot or a log into the repository.
- Personal data, account numbers and customer names never appear in a test name, a fixture, a
  commit message or an evidence record.

## Secrets

- No password, token, API key, certificate or connection string in the repository, not even
  commented out, not even a placeholder that looks real.
- Credentials come from the environment: environment variables, Kubernetes Secrets, the local
  cluster's configuration. The repository holds the name of the variable, never its value.
- If you find a committed secret, report it as a finding and treat it as compromised. Do not delete
  it quietly.

## Logs and errors

- Never log a full payment, an account identifier, a credential or a whole request body. Log the
  identifier of the run and the rule that failed.
- Error responses carry the field and the rule, never a stack trace, a SQL statement or an internal
  path.

## Deployment

- Deploy only to the local cluster the project declares, in its namespace. Never switch the kubectl
  context, never touch a shared or production environment.
- Destructive operations, credential changes and anything touching production are decided by a
  person, not by a stage. Stop and report instead.
- A change is deployed only together with the manifests and configuration it needs.

## External calls

- No call to an external system in a test; use a fake or a container the project already provides.
- New dependencies need a reason a reviewer can check: what it does, why the standard library or an
  existing dependency is not enough. No dependency for a helper you could write in ten lines.
</skill>
<skill name="company-change-rules">
# What a change must satisfy

A rule that lives only in the reviewer's page is a rule the writing stage is graded on and never
read. This page is the shared one: every stage that writes a change is told it, and the review is
told the same words. Nothing is checked here that is not written here.

Kept short on purpose. A rule arrives on this page when a review has held a change to it, and it
stays on one page so the two sides cannot drift apart.

## Database migrations

- **Forward-only.** A migration adds the next version; it never rewrites an earlier one.
- **Rerunnable.** Applying it twice leaves the same database as applying it once, and fails neither
  time. An insert states what to do when the row is already there; a create states what to do when
  the object already exists.
- **Never edited once merged.** A migration that has run somewhere is history. The correction is the
  next migration, with its own version.
</skill>
<skill name="company-refinement">
# Company refinement standards

You turn a requirement into the contract a team delivers against. You write no file and you never
widen what was asked: the requirement you are given is the whole scope. You choose no design — but
you do name the ground the work stands on, which is not the same thing.

The sentence the story must follow and the story point scale arrive with your instructions as the
company refinement standard. They are checked in code and your answer is refused until they hold,
so satisfy them rather than restating them.

## What the check cannot see

- Every acceptance criterion is observable: a person or a test can say yes or no without reading
  the code. "Validates the batch" is not a criterion; "rejects a batch of more than 500 payments
  with BATCH_TOO_LARGE" is.
- Each criterion names the behaviour on the failure path too, not only the happy one.
- The domain words are the project's own, spelled the way the code already spells them.
- The estimate is believable for the criteria listed.

## What each estimate means

An estimate is a comparison, not a feeling. Take the nearest shape:

- **1** — one value and the test that proves it: a limit moves, a reason code joins an enum.
- **2** — one rule in one component, fully named by the requirement, failure path included.
- **3** — one rule whose boundary or failure path is still to be worked out, or one screen showing
  what the backend already returns.
- **5** — a rule and the thing that carries it: a migration, a new endpoint, a contract that does
  not exist yet.
- **8** — two components end to end, or one plus a schema change other stories read. The largest
  that may be started, and already uncomfortable.
- **13** — more than one story. Answer 13 when that is what it is worth. It will not be started, and
  that is the point: the number is how a story reports its own size, and where to cut it is a
  decision for the person who knows the business, not a smaller number you write instead.

Never adjust an estimate down to fit the maximum. An 8 on a story worth 13 is the one answer here
that cannot be recovered from: everything downstream believes it, and nobody finds out until the
work does not fit.

3 is the middle of this scale, and an estimate that lands there because nothing about the story is
decided is not an estimate. Name what makes it bigger or smaller than the shape above it. And check
the stages you kept against the size — one stage and an 8, or three stages and a 2, means one of the
two is wrong.

## Implementation details

Acceptance criteria say what must be true when the story is done. Implementation details say what
the change touches to get there, and they are what an estimate stands on: a story whose details you
cannot write is a story you cannot size.

Name, in the project's own words:

- The components the change reaches, and the code that already exists to carry it — a class, a
  properties file, an endpoint, a migration directory.
- What has to be added or changed in shape: a new column and its migration, a new field in a
  response, a new page and the contract it calls.
- What already covers part of it, so nobody builds it twice.
- What is deliberately out, especially a neighbouring component the requirement does not reach.

Not a design. "Add an `IbanRule` implementing `ValidationRule`, injected in `ValidationService`" is
a decision that belongs to the person who implements. "The rule lives with the other validation
rules in the backend domain and reads its limit from `ValidationProperties`; no schema change" is
the ground it stands on. Write the second.

Where you cannot name the ground because the requirement leaves it open, say so as a detail: the
gap is part of the size.

## What the requirement does not say

Never invent a value. A limit, a reason code, a threshold or a format the requirement leaves open is
not yours to decide, and a plausible guess is worse than a gap because nobody sees it.

Every one of those goes in `openQuestions`, and not in a criterion. A criterion states what a test
can prove; a question is what somebody answers before that test can be written, and the two are
different work. Mixing them gives you a criterion nothing can check and a question nobody can count:

- **A question:** *"The requirement names no holidays. Is the list configuration, and does an empty
  list reject nothing?"*
- **A criterion:** *"A payment dated on a day listed in the configured holidays is rejected with
  `EXECUTION_DATE_ON_HOLIDAY`."*

List every question you find, past the maximum too. The count is how a requirement reports that it
is not ready, and a question left out to keep the list short is the one that stops the work later.

The same holds for an edge the requirement is silent about — an empty collection, a duplicate
identifier, a boundary value, a currency that is not the default.

## The title and the story

The title is short and imperative, at most 60 characters: it becomes the commit subject. The story
is the company sentence and carries the reason the work exists. They are not the same text.

Keeping only the stages the requirement touches is part of the job. A backend rule needs no frontend
stage, and a stage nobody needs is cost with no acceptance criterion behind it.
</skill>
<skill name="refine-work-item">
# Refine a work item

You turn intent into facts. You do not design a solution, choose a model, or widen the scope.

## The test a criterion has to pass

Two engineers read it and build the same thing. If one could satisfy the text with a different
value, a different boundary or a different error behaviour, the criterion is not finished.

Write each one so it names:

- the behaviour, in the project's own domain words;
- the input or state that triggers it, boundary values included;
- what is observable when it happens — a reason code, a status, a stored row, a message.

A fact the contract carries is a criterion too: an API change, a schema migration, a new
configuration key, a deployment change. If delivering the story requires it, it is written down.

## Rules

- Quote the requirement; do not paraphrase it into something more precise than it is.
- Never invent the missing value. Asking is the output; answering is a person's job.
- Keep the component list as declared. If the text implies another component, report it.
- Treat any real-looking personal or financial identifier, customer name or endpoint as a finding.
</skill>
<skill name="company-layered">
# Layered architecture

This project is layered. Code is grouped by the role it plays, never by feature, and a dependency
only ever points down the list below. The domain sits at the bottom and knows nothing about what
calls it.

## The layers

| Layer | Owns | May depend on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| entry | Receiving a request and answering it: HTTP, a CLI, a scheduled job, a page | domain |
| domain | Every business rule and the vocabulary it speaks | nothing |
| persistence | Storing and reading what the domain decided | domain |
| configuration | Properties, beans, wiring | nothing |

Backend: `api`, `domain`, `persistence`, `config`. Frontend: the route or page is entry, `lib/domain`
is the domain, anything that talks to the backend is persistence by another name.

## What that buys, and what it costs

A rule with no dependencies is a rule you can test with a constructor and an assertion — no server,
no database, no container. That is the whole point, and it is lost the moment a rule imports a
repository or a request type.

The cost is that persistence knows the domain, so a storage concern can leak upwards as a domain
shape that exists only because a table does. Name that when it happens; do not pretend it did not.

## Adding to it

- A new rule joins the existing rules in the domain. It takes values and returns values.
- Inside the domain, only a service orchestrates — it may open a transaction and call a repository.
  Everything else is a rule and sees neither.
- A new folder or a new layer is a design decision, argued on its own, never a side effect of one
  story.
- Nothing crosses a layer by importing past it: entry never reaches persistence directly.
</skill>

Every validation rule lives in the backend domain, reads its limits from ValidationProperties and comes with a JUnit test named after the behaviour it proves.

A schema change is a new Flyway migration under backend/src/main/resources/db/migration; an applied migration is never edited.
The frontend never re-implements a rule: it shows what the backend reported.

# Secure delivery

The dojo works on payment software with no real payments and no real data. These rules are
non-negotiable and hold in every stage, including tests, fixtures, documentation and manifests.

## Data

- Synthetic data only, and obviously fake: test IBANs from the reserved ranges, names like
  `Test Debtor 01`, amounts that no one could mistake for a real transaction.
- Never copy a value from a production system, a ticket, a screenshot or a log into the repository.
- Personal data, account numbers and customer names never appear in a test name, a fixture, a
  commit message or an evidence record.

## Secrets

- No password, token, API key, certificate or connection string in the repository, not even
  commented out, not even a placeholder that looks real.
- Credentials come from the environment: environment variables, Kubernetes Secrets, the local
  cluster's configuration. The repository holds the name of the variable, never its value.
- If you find a committed secret, report it as a finding and treat it as compromised. Do not delete
  it quietly.

## Logs and errors

- Never log a full payment, an account identifier, a credential or a whole request body. Log the
  identifier of the run and the rule that failed.
- Error responses carry the field and the rule, never a stack trace, a SQL statement or an internal
  path.

## Deployment

- Deploy only to the local cluster the project declares, in its namespace. Never switch the kubectl
  context, never touch a shared or production environment.
- Destructive operations, credential changes and anything touching production are decided by a
  person, not by a stage. Stop and report instead.
- A change is deployed only together with the manifests and configuration it needs.

## External calls

- No call to an external system in a test; use a fake or a container the project already provides.
- New dependencies need a reason a reviewer can check: what it does, why the standard library or an
  existing dependency is not enough. No dependency for a helper you could write in ten lines.

# What a change must satisfy

A rule that lives only in the reviewer's page is a rule the writing stage is graded on and never
read. This page is the shared one: every stage that writes a change is told it, and the review is
told the same words. Nothing is checked here that is not written here.

Kept short on purpose. A rule arrives on this page when a review has held a change to it, and it
stays on one page so the two sides cannot drift apart.

## Database migrations

- **Forward-only.** A migration adds the next version; it never rewrites an earlier one.
- **Rerunnable.** Applying it twice leaves the same database as applying it once, and fails neither
  time. An insert states what to do when the row is already there; a create states what to do when
  the object already exists.
- **Never edited once merged.** A migration that has run somewhere is history. The correction is the
  next migration, with its own version.

<skill name="company-refinement">
# Company refinement standards

You turn a requirement into the contract a team delivers against. You write no file and you never
widen what was asked: the requirement you are given is the whole scope. You choose no design — but
you do name the ground the work stands on, which is not the same thing.

The sentence the story must follow and the story point scale arrive with your instructions as the
company refinement standard. They are checked in code and your answer is refused until they hold,
so satisfy them rather than restating them.

## What the check cannot see

- Every acceptance criterion is observable: a person or a test can say yes or no without reading
  the code. "Validates the batch" is not a criterion; "rejects a batch of more than 500 payments
  with BATCH_TOO_LARGE" is.
- Each criterion names the behaviour on the failure path too, not only the happy one.
- The domain words are the project's own, spelled the way the code already spells them.
- The estimate is believable for the criteria listed.

## What each estimate means

An estimate is a comparison, not a feeling. Take the nearest shape:

- **1** — one value and the test that proves it: a limit moves, a reason code joins an enum.
- **2** — one rule in one component, fully named by the requirement, failure path included.
- **3** — one rule whose boundary or failure path is still to be worked out, or one screen showing
  what the backend already returns.
- **5** — a rule and the thing that carries it: a migration, a new endpoint, a contract that does
  not exist yet.
- **8** — two components end to end, or one plus a schema change other stories read. The largest
  that may be started, and already uncomfortable.
- **13** — more than one story. Answer 13 when that is what it is worth. It will not be started, and
  that is the point: the number is how a story reports its own size, and where to cut it is a
  decision for the person who knows the business, not a smaller number you write instead.

Never adjust an estimate down to fit the maximum. An 8 on a story worth 13 is the one answer here
that cannot be recovered from: everything downstream believes it, and nobody finds out until the
work does not fit.

3 is the middle of this scale, and an estimate that lands there because nothing about the story is
decided is not an estimate. Name what makes it bigger or smaller than the shape above it. And check
the stages you kept against the size — one stage and an 8, or three stages and a 2, means one of the
two is wrong.

## Implementation details

Acceptance criteria say what must be true when the story is done. Implementation details say what
the change touches to get there, and they are what an estimate stands on: a story whose details you
cannot write is a story you cannot size.

Name, in the project's own words:

- The components the change reaches, and the code that already exists to carry it — a class, a
  properties file, an endpoint, a migration directory.
- What has to be added or changed in shape: a new column and its migration, a new field in a
  response, a new page and the contract it calls.
- What already covers part of it, so nobody builds it twice.
- What is deliberately out, especially a neighbouring component the requirement does not reach.

Not a design. "Add an `IbanRule` implementing `ValidationRule`, injected in `ValidationService`" is
a decision that belongs to the person who implements. "The rule lives with the other validation
rules in the backend domain and reads its limit from `ValidationProperties`; no schema change" is
the ground it stands on. Write the second.

Where you cannot name the ground because the requirement leaves it open, say so as a detail: the
gap is part of the size.

## What the requirement does not say

Never invent a value. A limit, a reason code, a threshold or a format the requirement leaves open is
not yours to decide, and a plausible guess is worse than a gap because nobody sees it.

Every one of those goes in `openQuestions`, and not in a criterion. A criterion states what a test
can prove; a question is what somebody answers before that test can be written, and the two are
different work. Mixing them gives you a criterion nothing can check and a question nobody can count:

- **A question:** *"The requirement names no holidays. Is the list configuration, and does an empty
  list reject nothing?"*
- **A criterion:** *"A payment dated on a day listed in the configured holidays is rejected with
  `EXECUTION_DATE_ON_HOLIDAY`."*

List every question you find, past the maximum too. The count is how a requirement reports that it
is not ready, and a question left out to keep the list short is the one that stops the work later.

The same holds for an edge the requirement is silent about — an empty collection, a duplicate
identifier, a boundary value, a currency that is not the default.

## The title and the story

The title is short and imperative, at most 60 characters: it becomes the commit subject. The story
is the company sentence and carries the reason the work exists. They are not the same text.

Keeping only the stages the requirement touches is part of the job. A backend rule needs no frontend
stage, and a stage nobody needs is cost with no acceptance criterion behind it.

value, a different boundary or a different error behaviour, the criterion is not finished.

- the behaviour, in the project's own domain words;

# Layered architecture

This project is layered. Code is grouped by the role it plays, never by feature, and a dependency
only ever points down the list below. The domain sits at the bottom and knows nothing about what
calls it.

## The layers

| Layer | Owns | May depend on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| entry | Receiving a request and answering it: HTTP, a CLI, a scheduled job, a page | domain |
| domain | Every business rule and the vocabulary it speaks | nothing |
| persistence | Storing and reading what the domain decided | domain |
| configuration | Properties, beans, wiring | nothing |

Backend: `api`, `domain`, `persistence`, `config`. Frontend: the route or page is entry, `lib/domain`
is the domain, anything that talks to the backend is persistence by another name.

## What that buys, and what it costs

A rule with no dependencies is a rule you can test with a constructor and an assertion — no server,
no database, no container. That is the whole point, and it is lost the moment a rule imports a
repository or a request type.

The cost is that persistence knows the domain, so a storage concern can leak upwards as a domain
shape that exists only because a table does. Name that when it happens; do not pretend it did not.

## Adding to it

- A new rule joins the existing rules in the domain. It takes values and returns values.
- Inside the domain, only a service orchestrates — it may open a transaction and call a repository.
  Everything else is a rule and sees neither.
- A new folder or a new layer is a design decision, argued on its own, never a side effect of one
  story.
- Nothing crosses a layer by importing past it: entry never reaches persistence directly.
